assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints that amplify and propagate shocks through asset prices and credit give a transparent mechanism for credit cycles. The framework underlies much of modern macro-finance and policy analysis of financial crises. It is conceptually foundational, not just widely cited.
assessment.attribution: The core contribution is the Kiyotaki-Moore credit-cycles model, so two laureates capture it cleanly. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the adjacent financial-accelerator strand, which overlaps with the 2022 recognition of Bernanke. I leave them out to keep the credit to the originating mechanism.
assessment.maturity: The central paper dates from the 1990s, and three decades of theory, quantitative macro and crisis-era evidence support it. Timing is ripe, with no remaining doubt about the idea's durability.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee sees this as sufficiently distinct from the 2022 banking and financial-crisis prize.
Whether the Gertler-Gilchrist financial-accelerator strand should share credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic panel GMM estimators are everyday tools across applied economics, in growth, labour, finance and industrial organisation. They solved a real identification and estimation problem with lagged dependent variables and unobserved heterogeneity. The impact comes from enabling a very large body of empirical work.
assessment.attribution: The credit is fairly clear: Arellano-Bond (1991), Arellano-Bover (1995) and Blundell-Bond (1998). Arellano's broader panel-data contributions are central. Blundell's presence overlaps with his labour-supply work in another ballot entry.
assessment.maturity: More than 25 years of use, and the weak-instrument and many-instrument limitations are well documented, which shows the method's scope and limits.
uncertainties: Whether Alonso-Borrego, Holtz-Eakin, Newey and Rosen or others deserve credit for predecessors.
Whether the many-instrument and proliferation problems weigh against a prize for the method.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Measuring how misallocation of inputs across heterogeneous firms lowers aggregate TFP changed the study of cross-country income gaps. It linked firm-level microdata to growth and development accounting and spawned a large literature on policy distortions.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) is the pivotal paper. Restuccia-Rogerson (2008) is a parallel contribution, but Rogerson is not on the credited list. Restuccia's own agricultural and development work is a separate strand, so I propose two names.
assessment.maturity: About 17 years of replication, extension and measurement debate. Sensitivity to measurement error and to what counts as a distortion is now well understood.
uncertainties: Disclosed conflict: I have a long-running collaboration with Klenow and work close to this literature, so my ranking should be discounted accordingly.
How much measured misallocation reflects measurement error or markup heterogeneity rather than true distortions.
Whether Restuccia and Rogerson-type credit should alter the laureate set.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data on intergenerational mobility changed how economists and policymakers measure opportunity. The work also supports credible quasi-experimental estimates of neighbourhood effects.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear leader, with Hendren and Friedman as core collaborators on the mobility and neighbourhood-effects papers. Katz's role on Moving to Opportunity is real but more peripheral to the data innovation. Credit within a large team is hard to separate.
assessment.maturity: Mostly 2014 onward. Impact is large, but long-run replication and scrutiny of the causal neighbourhood and mobility estimates are still developing. Probably early compared with the older entries.
uncertainties: Whether the contribution is primarily measurement and data rather than new theory or method.
Whether the Committee prefers to wait for more long-run validation.
Team-based attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities is the workhorse of monetary-policy analysis. It is highly influential in central banks, and the rule-based policy view built on it is a major conceptual shift.
assessment.attribution: The attribution problem is severe: Calvo (pricing), Taylor (rules and staggered contracts), Woodford, Gali and others (synthesis), and Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans and Smets-Wouters (estimated models). Three names cannot cover this fairly. Any selection leaves out major contributors.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with decades of use and revision. The framework was challenged and extended after 2008 and 2020, but remains central.
uncertainties: Three-laureate cap against an eight-name field.
Overlap with earlier prizes on rational expectations and macro policy (Lucas, Sargent, Kydland-Prescott).
Whether the Committee would see it as a consensus synthesis rather than a single discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting reoriented trade theory and empirics toward within-industry reallocation and new gains-from-trade channels. It connects trade to productivity and micro data, and sits close to the firm-dynamics and growth agenda.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the key model. Helpman's contributions run from monopolistic competition in trade to Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exports versus FDI. Redding's work is influential but more recent and builds on this base. Krugman's earlier prize partly covers the preceding new trade theory.
assessment.maturity: Over 20 years of testing and extension, so timing is mature. Krugman's 2008 prize raises the question of how far this is a separate discovery.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats this as a distinct advance beyond Krugman's recognised work.
Whether Redding or Bernard-Jensen work on exporter facts deserves inclusion.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Evidence on the China shock and on technology and task-based labour demand reshaped debate on trade, inequality and adjustment costs. The empirical findings have had unusual influence on policy and public discourse.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock papers are credited to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The task framework includes Autor, Levy, Murnane and Acemoglu-Autor, with Acemoglu outside this ballot entry, so the credited trio does not capture the full task literature. Katz's skill-premium work is a separate strand.
assessment.maturity: The main results date from 2013 to 2016. Scrutiny of the identification and of long-run persistence is ongoing, and the 2024 recognition of AJR and 2021 recognition of credibility methods overlap in part.
uncertainties: Robustness of the shift-share identification and of the magnitudes.
Whether the task-framework credit is misaligned with the credited trio.
Fit with the 2023 Goldin prize on labour markets, if that matters to the Committee.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model gave a tractable and widely used foundation for bargaining, with applications in labour, trade and macro search models. Bargaining in markets connects it to decentralised exchange.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (1982) is the pivotal paper, with Rubinstein-Wolinsky (1985) on market bargaining. Binmore's contributions (including the Nash program and the Binmore-Rubinstein-Wolinsky 1986 paper) are substantive, but the three-name cap and tighter attribution favour the first two. Stahl's earlier related work and the Nash-program lineage complicate credit.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature, more than 40 years of use. The age of the laureates and the existing game-theory prizes (Nash, Harsanyi, Selten, Aumann, Schelling, Myerson, Maskin) are relevant to how the Committee weighs urgency.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee views bargaining theory as sufficiently distinct from already-honoured game theory and mechanism design.
Binmore's omission.
